title: Chapter 24 — The Advocate
paragraphs: Since Queequeg and I are now properly launched in this business of whaling, and since whaling has somehow come to be seen by people on land as a rather unpoetic and disreputable trade, I am anxious to convince you landlubbers of the injustice done to us whale hunters.

First, it may seem unnecessary to establish the fact that, among the general public, whaling is not considered on the same level as the so-called liberal professions. If a stranger were introduced into any mixed gathering of city society, it would hardly raise the general opinion of his merits to present him as a harpooner. And if, in imitation of naval officers, he were to add the letters S.W.F. (Sperm Whale Fishery) after his name on his business card, that would be considered extremely presumptuous and ridiculous.

No doubt one main reason the world refuses to honor us whalemen is this: people think that, at best, our occupation amounts to a butchering sort of business, and that when we're actively at work, we're surrounded by every kind of filth. Butchers we are — that's true. But butchers, too, and butchers of the bloodiest badge, have been all the military commanders whom the world invariably loves to honor. And as for the alleged uncleanliness of our business, you'll soon be let in on certain facts that until now have been pretty generally unknown, and which, on the whole, will triumphantly place the sperm whale ship at least among the cleanest things on this tidy earth. But even granting the charge to be true — what messy, slippery decks of a whale ship can compare with the unspeakable carrion of those battlefields from which so many soldiers return to drink in the applause of every lady? And if the idea of danger so greatly enhances the popular admiration of the soldier's profession, let me assure you that many a veteran who has freely marched up to a cannon battery would quickly recoil at the sight of a sperm whale's vast tail fanning the air above his head into eddies. For what are the terrors of man, which we can understand, compared with the interlinked terrors and wonders of God!

But though the world looks down on us whale hunters, it unknowingly pays us the deepest tribute — indeed, an overwhelming devotion! For almost all the candles, lamps, and tapers that burn around the globe burn, like offerings before so many shrines, to our glory!
But look at this from other angles. Weigh it on every scale. See what we whalemen are and have been.

Why did the Dutch in De Witt's time have admirals of their whaling fleets? Why did Louis XVI of France, at his own personal expense, fit out whaling ships from Dunkirk, and politely invite a score or two of families from our own island of Nantucket to that town? Why did Britain, between the years 1750 and 1788, pay her whalemen upwards of £1,000,000 in bounties? And lastly, how is it that we American whalemen now outnumber all the rest of the world's whalemen banded together; sail a navy of upwards of seven hundred vessels, manned by eighteen thousand men, consuming $4,000,000 a year, the ships worth $20,000,000 at the time of sailing; and every year bring into our harbors a well-reaped harvest of $7,000,000? How does all this come about, if there isn't something mighty in whaling?
But that's only half of it. Look again.

I freely assert that the cosmopolitan philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has worked more powerfully upon the whole broad world, taken all together, than the high and mighty business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so continuously momentous in their consequences, that whaling may well be regarded as that Egyptian mother who bore offspring that were themselves pregnant from her womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to catalogue all these things. Let a handful be enough. For many years past the whale ship has been the pioneer in ferreting out the remotest and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and archipelagoes that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor and glory of the whale ship, which first showed them the way and first interpreted between them and the savages. They may celebrate as they like the heroes of Exploring Expeditions, your Cooks, your Krusensterns; but I say that scores of anonymous captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great as your Cook and your Krusenstern, and greater. For in their unaided, empty-handed state, in heathenish, shark-filled waters and by the beaches of unrecorded, javelin-throwing islands, they battled with virgin wonders and terrors that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not willingly have dared. All that is made such a flourish of in the old South Sea Voyages was only the lifelong commonplace of our heroic Nantucketers. Often, adventures to which Vancouver devotes three chapters, these men thought unworthy of being set down in the ship's ordinary log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

Until the whale fishery rounded Cape Horn, no trade but colonial, and hardly any contact but colonial, was carried on between Europe and the long line of wealthy Spanish provinces on the Pacific coast. It was the whaleman who first broke through the jealous policy of the Spanish crown regarding those colonies. And if space allowed, it could be clearly shown how, from those whalemen, there at last came the liberation of Peru, Chile, and Bolivia from the yoke of Old Spain, and the establishment of the eternal democracy in those parts.

That great America on the other side of the globe, Australia, was given to the enlightened world by the whaleman. After its first blunder-born discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long shunned those shores as pestilently barbarous; but the whale ship called there. The whale ship is the true mother of that now mighty colony. Moreover, in the infancy of the first Australian settlement, the emigrants were several times saved from starvation by the benevolent biscuit of a whale ship that luckily dropped anchor in their waters. The countless islands of all Polynesia confess the same truth, and pay commercial homage to the whale ship, which cleared the way for the missionary and the merchant, and in many cases carried the first missionaries to their destinations. If that double-bolted land, Japan, is ever to become hospitable, it is the whale ship alone that will deserve the credit — for she is already on the threshold.

But if, despite all this, you still insist that whaling has no aesthetically noble associations, then I am ready to shiver fifty lances with you on that point, and unhorse you with a split helmet every time.
The whale has no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler, you say.

The whale no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler? Who wrote the first account of our Leviathan? Who but mighty Job! And who composed the first narrative of a whaling voyage? Who but no less a prince than Alfred the Great, who with his own royal pen took down the words of a man named Other, the Norwegian whale hunter of those times! And who delivered our glowing eulogy in Parliament? Who but Edmund Burke!
True enough, you say, but whalemen themselves are poor devils; they have no good blood in their veins.

No good blood in their veins? They have something better than royal blood there. The grandmother of Benjamin Franklin was Mary Morrel, afterward, by marriage, Mary Folger, one of the old settlers of Nantucket and the ancestress of a long line of Folgers and harpooners — all kith and kin to noble Benjamin — who to this day are darting the barbed iron from one side of the world to the other.
Fine, you say, but everyone agrees that whaling somehow just isn't respectable.
Whaling not respectable? Whaling is imperial! By old English statutory law, the whale is declared "a royal fish."*
Oh, that's in name only! The whale itself has never figured in anything grand or imposing.

The whale never figured in anything grand or imposing? In one of the mighty triumphs given to a Roman general upon his entry into the world's capital, the bones of a whale, brought all the way from the Syrian coast, were the most conspicuous object in the cymbal-clashing procession.*
*See later chapters for something more on this subject.
All right, since you bring it up. But say what you will, there's no real dignity in whaling.

No dignity in whaling? The very heavens bear witness to the dignity of our calling. Cetus is a constellation in the southern sky! Enough said! Jam your hat down firmly in the presence of the Czar, and take it off to Queequeg! Enough said! I know a man who, in his lifetime, has taken three hundred and fifty whales. I consider that man more honorable than that great captain of antiquity who boasted of taking as many walled towns.

And as for me, if by any possibility there is some as yet undiscovered prime quality in me; if I ever deserve any real reputation in that small but lofty, hushed world to which I might not unreasonably aspire; if hereafter I do anything that, on the whole, a man would rather have done than have left undone; if, when I die, my executors — or more accurately, my creditors — find any precious manuscripts in my desk, then here and now I ascribe all the honor and the glory to whaling in advance; for a whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.
